content: Efforts should be made to enhance reporting and monitoring systems for immunization programs to improve the quality of data on birth doses. The birth dose of vaccines should be followed by two or three additional doses to complete the primary immunization series. For women co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV), tenofovir-based antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HBV. This should be combined with a three-dose HBV vaccination schedule for all infants, including a timely birth dose. In cases of HIV and uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, artemisinin-based combination therapies should be carefully selected. Artemisinin + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine should be avoided in individuals on co-trimoxazole, and artemisinin + amodiaquine should be avoided in those on efavirenz or zidovudine. For individuals co-infected with visceral leishmaniasis and HIV in Eastern Africa, a regimen of liposomal amphotericin B (up to 30 mg/kg over six doses) combined with miltefosine (100 mg/day for 28 days) is conditionally recommended. In South-East Asia, the same regimen is recommended, but miltefosine is administered for 14 days. Secondary prophylaxis is advised after the first episode of visceral leishmaniasis in all co-infected individuals. For women living with HIV, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method for cervical cancer, rather than visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology. Existing programs using cytology should continue until HPV DNA testing becomes operational, while programs using VIA should transition rapidly due to quality assurance challenges. HPV DNA testing with triage is preferred over testing without triage. Triage options include partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology, depending on feasibility and resources. Cervical cancer screening should begin at age 25 for women living with HIV, with regular intervals of 3–5 years when using HPV DNA testing. For women over 50, screening can be stopped after two consecutive negative results. VIA and ablation treatments are unsuitable for postmenopausal women due to poor visualization of the transformation zone. Priority should be given to screening women aged 25–49, and postmenopausal women aged 50–65 who have never been screened should also be prioritized if resources allow. Mothers living with HIV are encouraged to breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue up to 24 months or longer while receiving full support for ART adherence. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months, followed by the introduction of complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding. Mixed feeding is not a reason to stop breastfeeding if ART is being used. These include case management, peer support, and quality improvement approaches. ART initiation should follow a people-centered care approach, focusing on individual needs and preferences. Rapid ART initiation, ideally within seven days of diagnosis, is strongly recommended, with same-day initiation offered to those ready to start. For individuals established on ART, clinical visits and medication refills should occur every 3–6 months, with six-month intervals preferred if feasible. Adherence support interventions, such as peer counseling, mobile phone reminders, and behavioral training, should be provided to improve adherence and virological suppression. HIV programs should implement community-level interventions to improve retention in care, including adherence clubs and tracing individuals who have disengaged from care. Task-sharing approaches for ART initiation and maintenance should be considered to optimize resource use and service delivery.
